{"type": "content", "content": "The report is written in `report/report.md` with eight figures and an appendix row for every problem. The system proves **24 of the 30 IMO-AG-30 problems**, and the independent checker accepts all 24 proofs. The prover, checker, search and learned prior were all built from scratch, offline, on two CPU cores.

| Configuration | Solved |
|---|---|
| Deduction without angle/ratio chasing (my own baseline) | 8 |
| Deduction with angle/ratio chasing | 15 (identical on 5 random diagrams per problem) |
| + one auxiliary point, any candidate ordering, 2,000 candidates | 23 |
| + two auxiliary points (beam search) | 24 (adds 2020 P1) |

Still unsolved: 2008 P1b, 2008 P6, 2011 P6, 2012 P5, 2019 P2, 2021 P3. For 2012 P5, 2019 P2 and 2021 P3, every one-point candidate and 2,000 two-point pairs fail. That points to missing deduction, most likely power-of-a-point / Pythagoras-type length reasoning, rather than a search shortfall.

- **Learned prior.** It is trained only on synthetic data, never on IMO labels. With 100 candidates it solves 21/30, against 17 for the hand-written heuristic and 16 for random order. Its median number of candidates to the first IMO proof is 33.5, against 567 and 824. At 2,000 candidates all three orderings end at 23, so the prior's value is cheaper search, not a higher final count.
- **Synthetic data.** 16,010 random diagrams produced 402,788 synthetic theorems with traced proofs (102,653 unique). Of the 3,818 whose proof uses an extra point and that I re-checked, 950 genuinely need it. That is about 2.4 orders of magnitude fewer theorems than AlphaGeometry's 10⁸, and about 3.8 orders fewer auxiliary-point examples. The prior's learning curve was still rising at the largest training size.
- **IMO 2004 P1 generalisation.** The audit of which premises each proof actually cites showed one proof never uses "O is the midpoint of BC". It holds with O any point, M any point of AB and N on AC with ON = OM. This holds on 200/200 random diagrams, including ones with O far from BC. It is proved with one auxiliary point (the circumcentre of AMN), accepted by the checker, and the proof transfers to 10/10 fresh diagrams. Dropping a premise the proofs do use fails on 0/30 diagrams in every case. A weaker generalisation also holds for 2002 P2b: O can be any point on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
- **Checker validation.** 835 of 840 deliberately corrupted proofs were rejected. I inspected the 5 that passed and all are equivalent to the original: two dropped citations were redundant, one "forged" fact is identical to a given premise, and two moved points never appear in the proof. All 25 auxiliary constructions re-prove on 4 fresh diagrams each (100/100).

Things that limit how far the results reach:
- **Diagram-assisted proofs.** About 24% of the angle-chasing steps in the final proofs (125 of 528) rely on the drawn diagram to pick which of two angle values holds, as do the non-degeneracy checks. The proofs are exact for the configuration drawn, not for every possible configuration.
- **Cited, not re-run.** I had no AlphaGeometry or geometry papers available (the supplied PDFs are off-topic). AlphaGeometry's 25/30, Wu's method's 10 and the medallist averages (bronze 19.3, silver 22.9, gold 25.9) come from memory of that paper. They should be checked against it before anyone relies on the comparison.
- **Candidate search.** Auxiliary points come from 14 hand-defined families. For the three largest problems the pool was capped at 200 per family, so some candidates were never tried there.
- **Small evaluation set.** The prior's IMO advantage is measured on only 8 problems that have a one-point proof, so those median ranks are noisy.

Everything else is under `outputs/`; `final_proofs/` holds one human-readable proof per solved problem."}
